items.text: Animals build their homes to achieve different living goals.
Bees build hives to store and protect food, spiders spin webs to catch prey and beavers build dams to create pools.
But, as you walk around a town or stroll along a countryside pathway, you may notice some unique homes up on the treetops - nests.

level1.label: 宾语

items.text: Like architects, birds carefully engineer their nests before building them.
A report named Architectural traditions in the structures built by cooperative weaver birds says that their designs are influenced by those before them.

level1.label: 宾语从句

items.text: A study released by iScience finds that birds follow a culture that gets passed down.

items.text: Not the high culture of art, literature and music, but an older process of transmitting traits and skills through generations.
Bird nest building: visions for the future, says that birds who are first-time builders will often copy familiar individuals, highlighting how important this individual, perhaps the parent, is.

items.text: These behaviours, though, can also change in response to pressures of natural selection, a term coined by Charles Darwin in his theory of evolution.

items.text: Competition is one of the three components of that theory.

level1.label: 表语

items.text: And it's not just in the human world where certain property locations are highly desirable.

items.text: Some species of birds even steal nest locations from others.
Studies at the Zoological Society of London have discovered that invasive species will compete with native birds for suitable trees to build their nests in.

items.text: Experiments published in Science Direct also show that most female birds look for fresh, green nests when choosing their mate.

level1.text: that most female birds look for fresh, green nests when choosing their mate

items.text: A report from RSPB further adds that in some species of birds, such as wrens, the male will build multiple nests from which the female can choose her favourite and even tidy it up.

items.text: This tells us that, like humans, the quality of a home, in addition to its location and cleanliness, can influence whether a pair of birds decide to live and start a family there.
